Tracing operational clues

I’m finding a strong new lead: Maier and Fludd share the same 1617 Galler/de Bry production shop. Farmer’s musical instructions add a procedural grammar—orientation, anchors, reversal, intervals, and return—that could guide the next primary-scan comparison.

Mapping musical instructions

I’ve found a strong new lead: Maier’s final fugues encode explicit reading operations—turning pages, starting from either end, using numbered pivots, reversing voices, and shifting by simple or compound intervals. I’m treating these as a historical instruction grammar, pending first-edition scan verification.

Mapping procedural clues

I’m finding a promising new lead: a same-year print network links Maier and Fludd, while Maier’s final Farmer-derived canons encode orientation, voice, starting point, reversal, midpoint, and octave-shifted intervals. I’m treating these as hypotheses until the original pages are checked.
